questions.stem: The Valley of the Kings, where Tutankhamun was buried, lies:
options: on the east bank of the Nile, beside the great temple of Karnak
in the Delta, close to the northern capital at Memphis
at Amarna, in the cliffs behind Akhenaten's new city
in desert hills on the west bank of the Nile at Thebes
questions.explanation: New Kingdom kings were buried in rock-cut tombs in a desert valley on the west bank at Thebes, the side of the setting sun linked with the dead. Karnak and Luxor temples stand on the east bank.

questions.stem: Why did New Kingdom kings choose the Valley of the Kings for their tombs rather than building pyramids?
options: There was no stone suitable for building near Thebes, so tombs were dug into sand
The valley was the only place where the Nile flood could not damage the burials
Hidden rock-cut tombs were harder to rob, and a pyramid-shaped peak rose above it
Pyramids had been banned by the priests of Amun after the fall of the Old Kingdom
questions.explanation: Pyramids had advertised royal burials to robbers, so New Kingdom kings cut concealed tombs in a remote valley. The peak of el-Qurn above it has a natural pyramid shape, which may have added to its appeal.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun was born with the name Tutankhaten. What did the change of name to Tutankhamun signal?
options: His adoption by the high priest of Amun as heir to the throne of Egypt
His victory over the Hittites in a campaign that was led by his general Horemheb
The move of the royal court from Thebes to Akhenaten's new city
A return to Amun and the traditional gods after the Amarna Period
questions.explanation: The name change from 'living image of the Aten' to 'living image of Amun' marked the restoration of the old gods early in his reign. The court moved away from Amarna, not towards it.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun came to the throne as a boy of about eight or nine. Which officials are thought to have held real power during his reign?
options: Ramesses, the vizier, and his son Seti, a commander of troops
Ay, a senior courtier, and Horemheb, commander of the army
Senenmut, the steward of Amun, and Ineni, the royal architect
Imhotep, the vizier, and Rekhmire, the mayor of Thebes
questions.explanation: Ay and Horemheb were the leading figures at Tutankhamun's court, and both later became king. Senenmut and Ineni served Hatshepsut and Thutmose I; Imhotep lived in the Old Kingdom.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun died young and left no surviving children. Who succeeded him as king?
options: Horemheb, who took the throne at once by leading the army to Thebes
Ankhesenamun, who ruled alone as king for a decade after his death
A Hittite prince, who married the widowed queen and ruled for years
Ay, the courtier who is shown burying him in his tomb painting
questions.explanation: Ay became king and is painted performing the Opening of the Mouth for Tutankhamun. Horemheb became king only after Ay. A Hittite text says a widowed Egyptian queen asked for a Hittite prince, but the prince died on the journey.

questions.stem: The king lists carved at Abydos under Seti I pass straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb. What does this omission best show?
options: The scribes at Abydos had not heard of any king who ruled at Amarna
Horemheb was the son of Amenhotep III and so followed him directly
Later kings treated the Amarna rulers, Tutankhamun among them, as illegitimate
Tutankhamun's reign was so very short that it was thought too brief to be recorded at all
questions.explanation: Akhenaten, his short-lived successors, Tutankhamun and Ay were left out because the Amarna Period came to be seen as a time of heresy. The gap is deliberate, not a lack of knowledge, and Horemheb was not Amenhotep III's son.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun's ancestry is often called a 'mystery of the pharaonic line'. Which statement best reflects the evidence?
options: DNA tests proved he was unrelated to the royal family and was chosen by the priests
A 2010 DNA study linked him to the KV55 mummy, but its identity is still debated
His tomb contains a stela naming Akhenaten and Nefertiti as his parents beyond doubt
Ancient king lists record his parentage, so there has never been any real debate
questions.explanation: No inscription clearly names his parents. A 2010 study of royal mummies linked him to the KV55 mummy, often identified as Akhenaten, and to a woman called the Younger Lady, but who those mummies were remains argued over.

questions.stem: Howard Carter's search for Tutankhamun's tomb was paid for by:
options: Theodore Davis, an American lawyer and collector
Lord Carnarvon, a wealthy English aristocrat
the Egyptian Antiquities Service in Cairo
the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York
questions.explanation: Lord Carnarvon funded Carter's work in the Valley of the Kings. Theodore Davis had held the earlier concession and believed, wrongly, that the valley was exhausted.

questions.stem: In which year did Howard Carter find the steps leading down to Tutankhamun's tomb?
questions.explanation: The first step was found in early November 1922. 1932 was roughly when Carter finished clearing the tomb, about ten years later.

questions.stem: Why had Tutankhamun's tomb stayed hidden for so long?
options: Its entrance lay under workmen's huts and rubble from a later royal tomb
It was cut into a cliff face far outside the Valley of the Kings
Its entrance was sealed with a false wall disguised as a natural rock face
It had been flooded by the Nile and buried under river silt until 1922
questions.explanation: Workmen's huts and rubble from cutting the nearby tomb of Ramesses VI covered the entrance, which helped protect it from later robbers. The tomb lies in the main valley, and the Nile flood does not reach it.

questions.stem: Carter's clearance of the tomb took about ten years. Which practice made his excavation more careful than most earlier work in the valley?
options: Objects were left in place and the tomb was opened to tourists unchanged
Only objects of gold were recorded, as the rest had little value to science
Each object was numbered, photographed in place and recorded before removal
All the objects were removed in a few weeks to protect them from robbers
questions.explanation: Carter's team, including the photographer Harry Burton and the chemist Alfred Lucas, recorded, photographed and conserved objects before moving them. This slow method is why the clearance took a decade.

questions.stem: Carnarvon died in Cairo in 1923, a few months after the tomb was opened. Newspapers spread the idea of a 'curse of the pharaohs'. How should a historian treat this story?
options: As an ancient Egyptian belief recorded in the Book of the Dead for royal tombs
As a press legend, since his death had a medical cause and Carter lived on for years
As reliable evidence, since a curse inscription was found carved over the tomb's door
As proof that the tomb contained dangerous poisons that had been left there by ancient priests
questions.explanation: Carnarvon died of an infection that followed an insect bite, and Carter lived until 1939. No curse inscription was found at the entrance; the story grew from newspaper rivalry and popular fascination.

questions.stem: Under the terms of the excavation, Carnarvon's heirs hoped to receive a share of the finds. The Egyptian government kept the whole collection. Why is this decision significant?
options: It reflected growing Egyptian control over its own heritage after 1922
It showed that the tomb's objects were judged to have no scientific value
It meant that all the objects were sold to museums across Europe instead
It proved that the tomb had been robbed of everything worth dividing
questions.explanation: Egypt became formally independent in 1922, and the authorities insisted that an intact royal tomb stay together in Egypt. This was a shift away from dividing finds with foreign excavators.

questions.stem: Which list gives the four rooms of Tutankhamun's tomb?
options: Antechamber, Annexe, Burial Chamber and Treasury
Pillared hall, sun court, sanctuary and chapel
Valley temple, causeway, mortuary temple and pyramid
Forecourt, hypostyle hall, offering room and shrine
questions.explanation: A stairway and corridor led to the Antechamber, with the Annexe off it; the Burial Chamber and Treasury lay beyond. The other lists describe temples or pyramid complexes.

questions.stem: Compared with the tombs of kings such as Seti I, Tutankhamun's tomb is small and only the Burial Chamber is painted. Which explanation do many Egyptologists give?
options: The priests of Amun refused to decorate the tomb of a former Aten worshipper
His larger tomb was destroyed by a flood before his funeral took place
He died unexpectedly young, so a smaller tomb was used and finished quickly
Kings of the late 18th Dynasty were forbidden to decorate their tombs
questions.explanation: His early death left little time, so many scholars think a small tomb, possibly not first meant for a king, was adapted and only the Burial Chamber decorated. Later Ramesside tombs such as Seti I's are long and fully decorated.

questions.stem: Seals on the tomb's doorways showed that they had been opened and resealed in antiquity. What does this evidence show?
options: The tomb was used again for the burial of Ay and his family in later years
Carter's workmen had entered the tomb secretly before it was officially opened
Robbers broke in soon after the burial, and officials then resealed the tomb
The tomb was opened every year so that priests could renew the food offerings left inside
questions.explanation: Robbers entered at least twice not long after the funeral, and necropolis officials restored order and resealed the doors. Gold rings knotted in a cloth, apparently dropped by a robber, fit this picture.

questions.stem: In the Burial Chamber, the king's mummy lay inside:
options: a mud-brick pyramid built in the middle of the Burial Chamber floor
a stone sarcophagus buried under the floor of the Antechamber
three nested coffins in a stone sarcophagus, inside four gilded shrines
a single wooden coffin placed in a niche cut into the chamber wall
questions.explanation: Four gilded wooden shrines nested around a stone sarcophagus, which held three coffins; the innermost was of solid gold. The layers protected the body and recreated the divine shrine.

questions.stem: The Treasury held a gilded shrine guarded by four goddesses, Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Selket. What did the shrine contain?
options: The papyrus copy of the Book of the Dead that Carter found intact
The statues of the king's ka, which guarded the Burial Chamber door
A calcite chest holding the king's embalmed organs in small gold coffins
The king's gold mask, which was kept apart from the body until the day of the funeral
questions.explanation: The canopic shrine held a calcite (Egyptian alabaster) chest with four compartments, each holding a small gold coffin containing an organ. The four goddesses protected the organs.

questions.stem: Which scene appears on the walls of Tutankhamun's Burial Chamber?
options: The king leading a chariot charge against the Hittite army at Kadesh
Workers cutting stone for the tomb under the eye of their foreman
The king and queen worshipping the Aten under its rays of light
Officials dragging the king's coffin on a sledge to the tomb
questions.explanation: The Burial Chamber shows the funeral procession, Ay performing the Opening of the Mouth, and the king welcomed by gods such as Nut and Osiris. Battle scenes at Kadesh belong to Ramesses II.

questions.stem: The back of the golden throne shows Ankhesenamun touching the king, with the sun disc of the Aten shining above them. Why is this scene useful evidence?
options: It suggests the throne was made while Aten imagery was still in royal use
It proves that Tutankhamun never abandoned the worship of the Aten
It shows that Ankhesenamun ruled Egypt as co-king with her husband
It records the date of their marriage in a hieroglyphic inscription
questions.explanation: The Aten disc and the couple's original Aten-based names point to manufacture early in the reign or before, in the Amarna style. Other objects show his return to Amun, so it cannot prove he kept the Aten faith.

questions.stem: A painted chest from the tomb shows Tutankhamun in his chariot defeating Nubian and Syrian enemies. How should a historian use it?
options: As an eyewitness record of a campaign that Tutankhamun led in person as a teenager
As evidence that Tutankhamun was too ill ever to ride in a chariot
As a scene copied from the Hittite archive describing his wars
As royal ideology of the king as conqueror, not proof that he fought
questions.explanation: Smiting and conquering enemies was a standard image of kingship. It may echo campaigns led by his generals, but by itself it does not show the young king fought.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun's tomb held more than 400 small figures called shabtis. What were they for?
options: To represent the servants who had been killed and buried with the king
To act as toys that the king had played with as a child at court
To mark the boundaries of the tomb so that robbers would stay out
To do the work the king might be called on to perform in the afterlife
questions.explanation: Shabtis were magical servants that would answer for the dead when labour was demanded in the afterlife. Royal servants were not sacrificed in New Kingdom burials.

questions.stem: The tomb contained chariots, bows, walking sticks, board games, clothing, food and wine. What does this range of goods best reveal about funerary beliefs?
options: The king expected to be reborn on earth as a new king of Egypt
Kings were buried with all their possessions so heirs could not inherit them
Only food mattered, and the rest of the goods were placed there for display
The afterlife was imagined as a continuation of life, needing everyday goods
questions.explanation: Egyptians equipped the dead with what they would need to live on, from food and drink to clothes, weapons and games. These objects also show royal life at the time.

questions.stem: Wine jars in the tomb were labelled with the year of the reign, the vineyard and the chief vintner. The latest labels date to about Year 9 or 10. What can a historian reasonably infer?
options: Tutankhamun was about ten years old when he died at Thebes
The tomb was robbed ten years after the burial, taking the newer wine
Tutankhamun probably reigned for about ten years before he died
The king was buried ten years after his death, once the wine had aged
questions.explanation: The labels give regnal years, so the latest date suggests he died in about his tenth year as king. As he came to the throne at about eight or nine, this fits a death at about eighteen or nineteen.

questions.stem: Flowers and fruits in the funerary wreaths, such as cornflowers and mandrake, ripen in Egypt in spring. What can this evidence suggest?
options: The tomb was robbed in spring, as robbers left the flowers behind
The wreaths were added by Carter's team when the coffins were opened
The burial probably took place in about March or April
The king died in spring, so he was buried within one week
questions.explanation: The plants in the wreaths point to a burial in spring. Since mummification took about seventy days, death would have come some weeks earlier, not in the same week.

questions.stem: A dagger from Tutankhamun's wrappings has an iron blade. A 2016 chemical analysis showed that the iron is unusual because it:
options: was smelted in Egypt from local ore in large furnaces
was imported from the Roman Empire many centuries later
had been coated in gold to stop it from rusting away
came from a meteorite, as shown by its high nickel content
questions.explanation: The blade's nickel and cobalt content matches meteoritic iron. Iron smelting was still rare in Egypt in this period, which is why such an object was precious.

questions.stem: During the funeral, a priest touched the mummy's face with special tools in the Opening of the Mouth ceremony. Its purpose was to:
options: test whether the heart was lighter than the feather of Ma'at
restore the dead person's senses for use in the afterlife
remove the brain through the nose before the body was wrapped
seal the coffin lid so that no evil spirit could enter the body
questions.explanation: The ritual restored the senses and powers of the body or statue for life in the afterlife. Removing the brain was part of embalming, and the weighing of the heart took place in the judgement before Osiris.

questions.stem: Egyptians believed a person had several spiritual parts. The ka was:
options: the name, which was carved on the outside of the coffin
the life force, which needed food offerings after death
the heart, which held a person's thoughts and deeds
the shadow, which guarded the tomb against robbers
questions.explanation: The ka was the life force that stayed with the body and fed on offerings. The ba, shown as a human-headed bird, could travel out of the tomb, and the akh was the transfigured spirit.

questions.stem: Mummification in the New Kingdom usually took about:
options: 7 days
30 days
one year
70 days
questions.explanation: The whole process, including drying the body in natron and wrapping it, took about seventy days. Herodotus and Egyptian texts both give this period.

questions.stem: What was natron used for in mummification?
options: Drying out the body by drawing moisture from the tissues
Colouring the skin to give the mummy a lifelike appearance
Gluing the linen wrappings together around the body
Filling the skull after the brain had been removed
questions.explanation: Natron, a natural salt, was packed around and inside the body to dry it, preventing decay. Resin, not natron, was used to coat the body and wrappings.

questions.stem: Embalmers poured large amounts of resin over Tutankhamun's mummy. What problem did this cause for Carter's team in 1925?
options: The resin hid all the amulets, so none were found in the wrappings
The hardened resin had fixed the mummy to the inside of the gold coffin
The resin had dissolved the gold mask, leaving only fragments to recover
The resin made the linen wrappings burst into flames as soon as they were exposed
questions.explanation: The resin set hard, gluing the body to the coffin and the mask. To free it, the team cut the mummy into pieces and used heated knives, damaging the remains. Many amulets and jewels were still found in the wrappings.

questions.stem: The first examination of Tutankhamun's mummy, by the anatomist Douglas Derry in 1925, concluded that the king:
options: lived to about forty years of age
died of malaria contracted in Nubia
died at about eighteen years of age
died of a blow to the back of the head
questions.explanation: Derry judged his age at death from the state of his bones and teeth. The murder theory came after X-rays in 1968, and malaria was identified by DNA in 2010.

questions.stem: X-rays taken in 1968 showed bone fragments inside Tutankhamun's skull, and some writers claimed he had been murdered. A CT scan in 2005 challenged this theory because it showed:
options: a healed fracture, so the injury had happened many years before he died
no bone fragments were present inside the skull at all
the fragments were probably broken after death, in embalming or in 1925
the skull was undamaged, so the X-rays had been taken of another mummy
questions.explanation: The scanning team concluded the loose fragments were probably dislodged after death, and found no sign of a fatal blow. The same scan drew attention to a fracture of the left thigh bone.

questions.stem: A 2010 study used CT scans and DNA analysis on Tutankhamun and other royal mummies. Which finding did it report?
options: Evidence of malaria, a deformed foot and bone disease in the foot
Evidence that the king was poisoned with arsenic by his successor
Proof that the king died from injuries suffered in a chariot crash in battle
Proof that the mummy in the tomb was not Tutankhamun at all
questions.explanation: The team found DNA of the malaria parasite, a clubfoot and bone disease in the foot, and suggested malaria combined with a leg fracture contributed to his death. Other researchers dispute parts of these conclusions.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Science has now solved how Tutankhamun died.' Which response best evaluates this claim?
options: The claim is correct, as his cause of death is recorded on a stela in the tomb
Studies have weakened some theories, but rival explanations remain
The claim is correct, as the 2005 scan proved the 1968 murder theory beyond doubt
The claim is wrong, as no scientific study of his body has ever been permitted
questions.explanation: Scans weakened the murder theory, but malaria, the leg fracture, disease and accident theories are still debated, partly because the body was damaged by embalmers and in 1925. No ancient text records how he died.

questions.stem: Since 2007 Tutankhamun's mummy has been displayed in his tomb in a climate-controlled glass case. Which ethical issue does this raise?
options: Whether the tomb should be filled in so that no one can see it again
Whether showing a dead person to tourists respects his beliefs
Whether the case allows scientists to remove samples without permission
Whether the king's body should be sold to a museum outside Egypt
questions.explanation: The case protects the remains from humidity and visitors' breath, but showing a human body to the public raises questions of respect, especially as Egyptians buried the dead to keep them hidden and whole.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an ethical issue in 21st-century scientific study of Tutankhamun's remains?
options: Once remains are in a museum, ethical questions about them no longer apply
Tests such as DNA sampling can damage remains, so benefits must be weighed
Scientific study is unethical only when the remains are less than a thousand years old
Egypt's laws forbid any scientific study of royal mummies by Egyptian scientists
questions.explanation: Sampling and handling can harm fragile remains, and decisions about who studies them and who controls results matter. Egyptian scientists led the 2005 and 2010 studies.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun is one of the most famous ancient Egyptians, although he was a minor king who died young. Which reason best explains his modern fame?
options: Ancient writers such as Herodotus described him as Egypt's greatest king
He built more temples than any other king of the New Kingdom
He led the armies that drove the Hyksos out of Egypt
His tomb was found almost intact, and its treasures toured the world
questions.explanation: His fame comes from the discovery of 1922 and its gold, publicised by the press and later by touring exhibitions. His actual reign left few monuments, and the Hyksos were expelled by Ahmose about two centuries earlier.

questions.stem: Images of Tutankhamun range from the frail boy with a walking stick to the golden warrior king. Which explanation best accounts for these differing representations?
options: Ancient sources disagree about him because Greek historians wrote his biography
Writers select from mixed evidence, such as his illnesses and royal images
Only one image is based on evidence; the other was invented in Hollywood films
The differences arise from two separate kings, both of whom were named Tutankhamun
questions.explanation: Medical studies of his body suggest illness and disability, while the objects in his tomb present the ideal of a strong king. Modern representations select and stress different parts of this evidence.
